title: Literals, new and the String pool

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, what does `String city = new String("New York");` give you?

options.text: The pool's existing "New York" object, if the pool already holds one
options.says: The page says new always creates a new object, separate from the pool.

options.text: A new String object on the heap, whatever the pool already holds
options.says: The page says using new always creates a new String object in heap memory, separate from the pool.

options.text: A new String object in the pool, which replaces any older equal one
options.says: The page says the object new creates is separate from the pool; it is not put into it.

questions.stem: With `String s1 = "Hello"; String s2 = "Hello";`, what does this page say `s1 == s2` gives, and why?

options.text: true, since both variables refer to one pooled object
options.says: The page says both literals refer to the same String object in the pool, so == is true.

options.text: false, since each literal makes an object of its own
options.says: The page says a literal reuses an identical String already in the pool.

options.text: true, since == on two Strings compares their characters
options.says: The page says == compares object references, not String contents; it is true here because the object is shared.

concepts: new String("...") always creates a new object outside the pool, while a literal reuses the pooled one.
Two equal literals refer to one pooled object, so == on them is true, while == compares references, not contents.
